mainQuests.deliverable: A spreadsheet or table with the calendar, the pass reward track with persona completion days, 2 event specs and a one-paragraph economy impact note. Post a screenshot and short thread publicly.
mainQuests.doneWhen: No event-soup days (at most 1 primary + 2 secondary events), no dead pass tiers, the regular persona finishes with 3–5 days to spare, every event lists a success metric, and the economy note exists.

mainQuests.title: Mock Design Test: 1-page feature spec under a time box
mainQuests.task: Simulate a studio take-home: 'Design a new feature for [a match-3 or midcore game] that increases D7 retention without hurting monetization.' Use GAMES: goal and KPI, assumptions, wireframes and flow, rules and edge cases, ethics check, analytics events, an A/B plan (hypothesis, primary and guardrail metrics, rough sample size via 16·p(1−p)/δ²) and MVP vs later scope. Strict 4-hour limit.
mainQuests.deliverable: A 1-page executive summary + 2–4 pages of detail with at least one wireframe or flow diagram. Ask a designer or community to review it as a hiring manager would, then add it to your portfolio.
mainQuests.doneWhen: Page 1 alone explains the feature, at least one visual flow exists, every number has a rationale, the test plan names a guardrail metric, and you stayed within 4 hours.

playLabs.lookFor: Every simultaneous event, timer and offer on the main screen. Which are solo and which are social (partner events, sticker trading)?
playLabs.question: How do the events feed each other, and is it clear what to do first, or is it event soup?

playLabs.lookFor: The pass screen (free vs premium track, instant value, chase reward) and the club/clan screen.
playLabs.question: What social actions take under 30 seconds, and which ones create obligation? Where does the pass place its strongest premium hook?

playLabs.game: Genshin Impact or Honkai: Star Rail
playLabs.lookFor: Taps from the banner to the odds/details page and the pull history, and how pity and the featured guarantee are explained.
playLabs.question: Would a new player understand the real cost of a guaranteed featured character from what the game shows?

playLabs.game: An ad-monetized casual game (e.g. Block Blast!, a hyper-casual chart-topper, or an Archero/Survivor.io-style hybrid)
playLabs.lookFor: Every ad moment: type (rewarded, interstitial, banner), trigger and reward.
playLabs.question: Which ads did you choose, which were forced, and did any appear at a frustrating moment?

retrieval.q: Name six IAP types and one design risk of each.
retrieval.a: Consumables (pay-or-lose feeling), durables (balance-breaking power, one-time revenue), cosmetics (need an audience), convenience (artificial friction suspicion), subscriptions (must deliver every period, easy cancel), bundles (need a hero item), starter packs (bad timing), LTOs (fake urgency), personalized offers (fairness and exploitation), passes (pass fatigue).

retrieval.q: Why is the first purchase so important, and when should a starter pack appear?
retrieval.a: It breaks the 'I don't pay' identity and payment friction, and repeat purchases become far more likely. Show it after the player understands item value (post-FTUE, often after the first wall): high value, low price, one time only.

retrieval.q: What is the decoy effect? Give a store example.
retrieval.a: A third option exists to make another look better. E.g. $9.99 = 1,000 gems, $19.99 = 2,200, $24.99 = 2,300, which makes the $19.99 look smart.

retrieval.q: Explain hard pity, soft pity and spark. Why does pity matter more than the average rate?
retrieval.a: Hard pity guarantees the top item by pull N. Soft pity raises rates after a threshold. Spark exchanges pull points for a chosen item. Pity caps the worst-case tail, where frustration and churn live.

retrieval.q: With a 1% rate and no pity, roughly what share of players still lack the item after 100 pulls?
retrieval.a: About 37% (0.99^100), and about 10% need ~230 or more pulls.

retrieval.q: Name four loot box rules or disclosure requirements and what they require.
retrieval.a: Apple and Google: odds before purchase. China: odds disclosure plus minors' limits. Japan: kompu gacha banned (2012). South Korea: mandatory disclosure (2024). Belgium: paid loot boxes can be gambling. UK: industry principles. Australia: higher age ratings (2024). Brazil: restrictions for minors (2025). Check current law.

retrieval.q: What is retroactive unlock in a battle pass, and why does it convert?
retrieval.a: Buying premium mid-season instantly grants all premium rewards for tiers already reached. The player sees a pile of loot they've already earned.

retrieval.q: How would you pace XP for a 30-day, 50-tier pass?
retrieval.a: Total XP = tiers × XP per tier. Pick a target persona (e.g. 5 days/week finishing ~day 26). Divide by active days to get a daily budget, split it across dailies, gameplay and weeklies, simulate casual, regular and hardcore personas, and add catch-up.

retrieval.q: When should you NOT show interstitials?
retrieval.a: During the FTUE, mid-action, after every loss, too frequently (use caps) and to payers.

retrieval.q: List six LiveOps event types and the main goal of each.
retrieval.a: Collection (engagement), leaderboard or race (competition), tournament (competitive spend), team/clan (social retention), community goal (togetherness), LTM (novelty and testing), boss raid (co-op), holiday (moments and offers), collab (buzz, new players), album (long arc + trading).

retrieval.q: What are the layers of a LiveOps calendar?
retrieval.a: Daily, weekly, main event rotation (~1–2 weeks), monthly (season or pass), quarterly (big updates), yearly (anniversary and holidays).

retrieval.q: Why are bucketed leagues more motivating than global leaderboards?
retrieval.a: In a small bucket every player has a realistic chance to place or promote. Global boards only motivate the very top.

retrieval.q: What are the five steps of an A/B test, and three classic pitfalls?
retrieval.a: Hypothesis, Metrics (primary + guardrails), Sample size, Duration, Decision rule. Pitfalls: peeking, small samples, novelty effect, metric-shopping, seasonality, contamination, short- vs long-term effects, Simpson's paradox, local maximum.

retrieval.q: Why do soft launches often use Canada/Australia/NZ and the Philippines?
retrieval.a: Canada/Aus/NZ are English-speaking proxies for US behaviour, cheaper and lower-profile, without burning the US. The Philippines offers cheap installs at volume to test tech and retention on low-end devices.

retrieval.q: Name four dark patterns, their healthy alternatives, and two reasons they backfire.
retrieval.a: Fake timers → honest timers. Currency fog → real-money prices. Friction for sale → challenge for fun. Accidental purchases → confirm steps. Streak guilt → freezes. They backfire through fines, store removal, refunds, reputation damage, trust collapse (lower LTV) and burnout churn.

feynman: Explain to a producer in 60 seconds how a F2P game keeps making money for five years without being evil. Cover the store with depth and contextual offers, a pass that sells the right to earn, rewarded ads for non-payers, a layered LiveOps calendar, social systems that keep friends together, A/B tests with guardrails, and why trust is worth more than any single offer.
